items.title: D3D12.X: resource_at keeps a PC texture for every view-at-address forever (~1 GB a minute on Linux/RADV)
items.body:
Part of #2688 (workstreams 3 and 5). Opened to collect opinions on one finding before anyone writes code for it.

**Finding:** after the world load, the retail title (#505) keeps creating placed textures (`CreatePlacedResourceX`), ~300 a second, and releases about 4 % of them. Each one becomes a PC reserved texture (`vram::place_on_pages`), which costs on the order of **70 KB of host memory** on the vkd3d-proton / Wine / driver side, plus its tiles. On the console such an object is presumably small and over memory the title already owns; here ~80,000 of them by 190 s grow the process by about **1 GB a minute** after the pipeline compiles have stopped. It is not a reference leak in XCL.

**Setup:** RX 7900 XT 20 GB, Mesa 26.2.5 RADV, i7-12700K, 24 GB RAM (title capped at 16 GB + 1 GB swap), Linux 7.2, Proton-CachyOS Wine 11, vkd3d-proton with dxil-spirv 53aac41. `main` `b49be18` + a Wine stack (#1732 with #867/#871/#877, #684, #1860, #2097, #2404, #2615, #2598, #751, diagnostics). `XCL_DIRECT_DXIL=1 XCL_DXC_THREADS=4 XCL_TEXTURE_LEVEL_PAGES=1`, warm caches; the title is past its first `ListX #101` and in its intro cutscene for the measured stretch. Local counters only (not a PR).

**Evidence** (details in #2688: [first](https://github.com/xcl-dev/xcl/issues/2688#issuecomment-7187299127), [second](https://github.com/xcl-dev/xcl/issues/2688#issuecomment-7188082689))

| | at 120 s | at 190–191 s | at 300 s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| reserved resources made (device creators) | 62,27

items.body:
*AI-assisted (Claude Code). Numbers and log lines only, no game data.*

**Measured: the title's CPU touches about 0.1-0.3% of what the copy-back writes into title memory. Nearly all the rest is read again only by the layer's own next refresh.**

This puts a number on README item (3), *"what shaders wrote left on the card until the title's processor reads it … being studied, nothing built"*. On this machine the copy-back and what follows it are the largest part of a frame.

## Setup

RTX 4090 (32-lane waves), driver 621.40, i9-14900K, 64 GB, Windows 11, Series X profile, diagnostics build. Tree: fork `main` `085ee7c` + #994 (and the #854/#993 below it) + #346 + #500 + #501, with the structure builder on (`VICTORY_BVH_BUILDER=1`), `RELAY=2` and the README's speed set. Scene: the barracks after the hand-off.

## Method

A diagnostic switch, `VICTORY_READ_CENSUS=1` (one commit on fork `main`: https://github.com/Yorivel/victory-fork/tree/diag/read-census):
- After `host::write_mapped` writes copied-back bytes into title memory, each 4 KiB page it wrote gets `PAGE_GUARD`, and a bit in a page bitmap.
- A vectored handler, registered first, takes guard hits on those pages. It clears the bit, counts the page once, and lets the access go on. The page is counted as **title read** or **title write** (`ExceptionInformation[0]`), or as **the layer's** when the faulting instruction is inside `victory.exe`.

items.title: LLM access equality for Project members
items.body:
I was heartened to learn about the [Dev Desktops](https://forge.rust-lang.org/infra/docs/dev-desktop.html). Through that initiative we ensure all Project members have access to the required hardware to work on and support the Project. This helps to *equalize* such access. People at big companies don't need these dev desktops: they already have enormous compute available to them. But not everyone is at one of these companies, so the dev desktops help to provide equal opportunity.

Today, in the Project, there's a similar disparity in how members can access LLM tools for use in Project work. Some Project members work for companies which give them an enormous budget; some members might be able to afford paying for it themselves; others cannot. That leaves a gap in *access*, when it comes to LLM tools.

The model providers, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, do offer programs where open source maintainers can apply for access. But many people may be reluctant to do that. For example, they may be reluctant to begin to rely on tools for Project work when access to those tools could be revoked arbitrarily by someone other than the Project itself. It seems that the Project should be in control of its own destiny here. It should be able to offer access to Project members in the same way that any other organization can offer these tools to their staff. When someone joins the Project, we should be able to turn on this access without simply hoping that another entity will approve that person'
